why: Before a launch, a new price or a campaign, companies want to know what customers think and do. Chargés d’études marketing (market research analysts) are hired to turn a business question into a study, run it with an institute or in-house survey tools, and deliver figures that lead to a decision. Interviews test your method: a clear brief, neutral questions, a sound sample and honest limits.
outcome: write a study brief with research questions, choose between desk research, qualitative and quantitative methods, run interviews and focus groups, write a questionnaire without bias, set quotas and compute a margin of error, clean survey data, read cross-tabs with significance, NPS and the classic studies, and present a report that ends with a recommendation.

lessons.title: What a chargé d’études does, and the brief
text: A chargé d’études marketing (market research analyst) answers business questions with data collected for the purpose: who buys, why, what customers think of a concept, a price, a brand. The job sits between the marketing team that has a decision to make and the field: survey tools, online panels, interviewers or a research institute. On the client side (an advertiser such as a food or cosmetics brand) you write briefs, manage institutes and turn results into recommendations; in an institute you design questionnaires, follow the fieldwork, process the data and write the report.

Every study starts with a decision, not with a questionnaire. “We want to know what customers think” is not a brief. “We must choose two of four recipes to launch in September” is. The research questions follow from the decision: who are the potential buyers, which concepts appeal to whom, at what price purchase intent drops. Each question in the final questionnaire should feed one research question; anything that does not is “nice to know” and makes the survey longer.

Desk research comes first because it is cheap and fast: internal data (sales, CRM, customer service logs, past studies), public statistics (INSEE in France, Eurostat in Europe), trade press, sector reports, competitors’ websites and annual reports. It often answers part of the brief and shows what the field study must add. Field research (primary data) then collects new information, either qualitative (a few people, in depth: why, how) or quantitative (many people, structured questions: how many, how much).

The brief is the contract between the marketing team and whoever runs the study. It states the context, the decision and its date, the research questions, the target, the expected method and deliverables, the timing and the budget. Institutes answer a brief with a proposal (method, sample, timing, price), and a good chargé d’études challenges the brief when the method cannot answer the question, for example a survey asked to predict exact sales of a product nobody has tasted.

In interviews you will be asked to describe how you would set up a study. Start from the decision, list the research questions, say what desk research would give you, then choose the method and the sample. That order shows you understand that a study is a tool for a decision.
points: Start from the decision the study must support, then write the research questions.
Desk research first: internal data, INSEE and other public statistics, past studies, competitors.
Qualitative answers why and how; quantitative answers how many and how much.
A brief states context, decision, research questions, target, method, deliverables, timing and budget.
Every question in a questionnaire must serve a research question.

example.code:
STUDY BRIEF - new plant-based dessert range
Context        Sales of the dairy dessert range flat for 2 years; plant-based
               competitors growing in supermarkets
Decision       Launch 2 of 4 recipe concepts in September, or not at all
Research Qs    1. Who buys plant-based desserts today, how often, why?
               2. Which concepts appeal most, to whom, and why?
               3. At what price does purchase intent drop?
Target         French adults 18-65 who buy desserts in supermarkets
Method         Desk research + 2 focus groups + online survey n = 1,000
Deliverables   Report with recommendation, cross-tabs, verbatims
Timing         Results by 15 June (go / no-go committee on 20 June)
Budget         To be confirmed with 2 options (with / without quali)
example.note: Every line of the brief can be checked later: did the study answer the research questions in time for the decision?

lessons.title: Qualitative studies: interviews and focus groups
text: Qualitative research explores motivations, perceptions, vocabulary and behaviours with a small number of people. It does not measure: you never say “60 % of participants” after eight interviews. It is used upstream of a survey (to find the right questions and answer options), to explore a new market, to understand why a number moved, or to improve a concept before testing it at scale.

In-depth interviews (entretiens individuels, usually semi-structured) last about 45 to 90 minutes with one person. They suit personal or sensitive topics (money, health), complex buying processes (B2B, a car) and people who are hard to gather (doctors, executives). Focus groups gather around 6 to 10 participants for about two hours with a moderator; group dynamics bring out reactions, disagreements and words, but also conformity: a strong participant can steer the others. Online versions (video interviews, online communities over several days) are now common.

The discussion guide structures the session without becoming a questionnaire. It goes from broad to specific (the funnel): daily habits, then the category, then the brand or concept, with open questions and neutral probes (“What makes you say that?”, “Can you tell me about the last time…?”). Stimuli such as concept boards, packs or ads are shown in a rotated order. Recruitment uses a screener questionnaire to find people who fit the target and to exclude, for example, people who work in marketing or for a competitor, or who took part in a study recently.

Analysis starts from transcripts or detailed notes. You code each passage by theme, fill an analysis grid (themes in rows, participants in columns), look for patterns, contrasts between profiles and surprises, and select verbatims: short quotes in the participant’s own words that illustrate a theme. The number of interviews is often decided by saturation: when new interviews stop bringing new themes, you have enough for that profile.

The deliverable is a set of insights and hypotheses, not figures. A typical sentence is “Participants hesitate because they doubt the taste of plant-based desserts, not because of price”, backed by verbatims, followed by what the quantitative phase should measure.
points: Qualitative explores why and how; it never gives percentages.
Interviews for personal topics and hard-to-reach people; focus groups for reactions and shared vocabulary.
The discussion guide goes from broad to specific, with open questions and neutral probes.
A screener recruits the right participants and excludes industry insiders.
Analysis: code by theme, analysis grid, verbatims, stop at saturation.

example.code:
DISCUSSION GUIDE - focus group, 2 hours, 8 participants
0:00  Welcome, rules, consent to record, warm-up (first names, hobbies)
0:10  Desserts in daily life: when, where, with whom? (broad, open)
0:30  Plant-based food: what comes to mind? experiences, doubts
0:50  Concept boards A-D: read alone, write first reactions, then share
      Probes: "What makes you say that?" "Who would this be for?"
1:30  Price and pack: what would you expect to pay? where in the store?
1:50  Final word: if you were the brand, what would you change?
2:00  Thanks, incentive
ANALYSIS: transcripts -> code by theme -> grid (theme x participant)
          -> key verbatims per theme -> "what this means for the brief"
example.note: The timings keep the session on track; the probes keep it open. The analysis plan is decided before the first group.

lessons.title: Writing a questionnaire without bias
text: A questionnaire is a measuring tool: if the questions are biased, the figures are wrong however large the sample. Questions come in a few types: closed single choice, closed multiple choice, scales (agreement, satisfaction, likelihood), numeric answers, rankings and open questions. Closed questions are easy to analyse; open questions bring words and surprises but cost coding time, so keep a few, at key moments.

A Likert scale measures agreement with a statement: Strongly agree, Agree, Neither agree nor disagree, Disagree, Strongly disagree. Five or seven points are common. An odd number keeps a neutral middle; an even number forces a side. Label every point, keep the same direction throughout the questionnaire and add “Don’t know” when people may genuinely not know. Answer lists must be exhaustive and mutually exclusive: age bands such as 18-24 / 25-34 never overlap, and “Other (please specify)” catches the rest.

The classic mistakes: leading questions (“Don’t you agree that…”, or a sentence that praises the brand first), double-barrelled questions that ask two things at once (“Is the app fast and reliable?”), vague time frames (“usually”, “recently”) instead of a precise period (the last 4 weeks), questions that rely on memory too far back, jargon the respondent does not know, and loaded words. Social desirability makes people overstate good behaviour (recycling, sport) and understate the rest; neutral wording and self-completion online reduce it.

Order matters. Earlier questions influence later ones, so ask spontaneous brand awareness before showing any brand, general satisfaction before detailed items, and sensitive or demographic questions near the end (except those needed for quotas, at the start). In lists, people tend to pick the first items they read (primacy) or the last ones they hear by phone (recency): rotate or randomise item order. Filters (skip logic) send each respondent only the questions that apply: a non-buyer does not rate a product they never bought.

Length kills quality. Long grids and surveys of more than about 15 to 20 minutes online bring tired, careless answers and drop-outs, especially on mobile, where many people answer. Test the questionnaire on a few people (a pilot or soft launch) before the full fieldwork: you will find unclear questions, missing answer options and broken filters.
points: Closed questions for counting, a few open questions for words and surprises.
Likert scale: labelled points, same direction, neutral middle on an odd scale.
Avoid leading, double-barrelled, vague and memory-heavy questions.
Spontaneous before aided, general before detailed, rotate lists, filters for who answers what.
Keep it short and pilot it before the fieldwork.

example.code:
BAD                                              BETTER
Don't you agree our new app is easier?        How easy or difficult is the new app
                                              to use? (Very easy ... Very difficult)
Is the app fast and reliable?                 Two questions: speed, then reliability
How much did you spend on desserts last year? How many dessert packs did you buy
                                              in the last 4 weeks?
Do you sometimes buy organic? (Yes / No)      How often do you buy organic desserts?
                                              (Every week / Every month / Less / Never)
Age: 18-25 / 25-35 / 35-50                    18-24 / 25-34 / 35-49 / 50-64 / 65+
example.note: Each fix makes the question neutral, single, precise and easy to answer. Age bands must not overlap.

lessons.title: Sampling: quotas, sample size and margin of error
text: The target population is the group the decision is about: French adults aged 18 to 65 who buy desserts in supermarkets, or IT decision makers in companies of 50 employees or more. You rarely interview all of them, so you draw a sample that should look like the population on what matters. Write the target precisely in the brief: it decides the screening questions, the cost (rare targets cost more per interview) and what the results can be generalised to.

In random (probability) sampling every member of the population has a known chance of being selected, and the statistics of sampling apply directly. It needs a list of the population (a customer file, for example) and costs more. In France, as in many countries, most consumer surveys use the quota method instead: the sample must reproduce the population’s structure on a few variables known from INSEE data, typically sex, age, occupation (PCS, the French socio-professional categories), region and size of town. Interviewers or the panel invite people until each quota cell is full.

Quota samples work well in practice, but strictly speaking the margin of error formula is made for random samples; institutes use it with quotas as an approximation. Say so in your limits. The margin of error for a proportion at 95 % confidence is 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) / n). With n = 1,000 and p = 50 % (the worst case), it is ±3.1 points: a result of 50 % means “between about 47 % and 53 %”. Precision improves with the square root of n: halving the margin needs four times the sample. The statistics course covers confidence intervals in more depth.

Sample size is chosen from the precision you need and, above all, from the sub-groups you want to read. A national sample of 1,000 adults gives only a few hundred people aged 18 to 34; with 250 of them, the margin is about ±6 points. If the decision depends on young buyers, boost that group (over-sample it) and weight it back in the total. A common rule in institutes is not to comment on a base under 30 respondents and to flag bases under about 50 to 100 as small.

Online access panels (people registered to answer surveys for small rewards) give fast, cheap national samples and are now the main source for consumer surveys. Their limits: panellists are volunteers who answer many surveys (professional respondents), some groups are under-represented (older people, people with little internet use, very busy executives), and quality depends on the panel’s checks. Telephone (CATI) and face-to-face (CAPI) still serve hard-to-reach targets.
points: Define the target population precisely: it drives screening, cost and conclusions.
Quota method: reproduce the population on sex, age, PCS, region and town size from INSEE data.
Margin of error at 95 %: 1.96 × √(p(1 − p)/n); ±3.1 points for n = 1,000.
Plan the sample for the sub-groups you must read; do not comment on tiny bases.
Online panels are fast and cheap but volunteers: state their limits.

example.code:
MARGIN OF ERROR at 95 %, observed share p = 50 %
n        margin
100      +/- 9.8 points
200      +/- 6.9 points
400      +/- 4.9 points
1,000    +/- 3.1 points
2,000    +/- 2.2 points
Excel: =1.96*SQRT(p*(1-p)/n)
Sample size for a margin E: =ROUNDUP(1.96^2*p*(1-p)/E^2,0)
p = 50 %, E = 3 points -> 1,068 respondents
QUOTA GRID (national adult sample, from INSEE population data)
Sex x age, occupation (PCS), region, size of town
example.note: Four times the sample halves the margin. The quota variables come from the official population figures.

lessons.title: Fieldwork, survey tools and GDPR
text: Surveys are run online (CAWI, computer-assisted web interviewing), by telephone (CATI) or face to face with a tablet (CAPI). Online is the default for consumer studies; telephone and face to face remain useful for people who are not online, for B2B decision makers and for long or complex interviews. For an in-house survey sent to your own customers (by e-mail or after a purchase), remember that only reachable and willing customers answer.

Tools range from simple to professional. Google Forms is free and quick for internal or small surveys, with basic logic. Typeform offers a pleasant one-question-at-a-time experience. SurveyMonkey covers most needs of marketing teams, with logic and simple analysis. Qualtrics is an enterprise platform with advanced logic, quotas, panels and dashboards. In France, Sphinx (Le Sphinx) is widely used by companies, public bodies and universities for both the questionnaire and the analysis. Institutes also use their own platforms and data processing tools.

GDPR applies as soon as answers can be linked to a person. Tell respondents who runs the survey, why, how long the data are kept and how to exercise their rights; rely on a valid legal basis (often consent for surveys) and let people stop at any time. Collect only what the study needs (data minimisation). Health, political opinions or religious beliefs are special categories with stricter rules: avoid them unless the study really needs them. In France the CNIL is the data protection authority and publishes practical guidance.

Anonymous and pseudonymous are not the same. Data are anonymous only when nobody can identify the respondent any more, even by combining answers (age + job + small town can identify someone). Replacing names by a respondent ID is pseudonymisation: the data are still personal data under GDPR. Results are reported in aggregate, and the client receives no individual answers linked to names unless respondents agreed to it, which is the usual rule of professional codes such as the ICC/ESOMAR International Code.

Data cleaning is part of the fieldwork. Speeders answer far faster than the median time; straight-liners give the same answer to every line of a grid; attention checks (“Select ‘Disagree’ for this line”) catch people who do not read; nonsense open answers and duplicates reveal bots or fraud. Agree the rules before the fieldwork, flag rather than delete on a single weak signal, replace removed interviews so that quotas stay full, and report how many were removed.
points: CAWI online, CATI by telephone, CAPI face to face.
Google Forms and Typeform for simple surveys, SurveyMonkey and Qualtrics for more, Sphinx widely used in France.
GDPR: information, legal basis, minimisation, special categories avoided, CNIL in France.
A respondent ID is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation.
Clean speeders, straight-liners, failed attention checks and duplicates with rules agreed in advance.

example.code:
DATA CLEANING FLAGS - online survey, 1,124 completes
Speeder        time < 1/3 of the median time (median 12 min)    41
Straight-liner same answer on every item of the 15-item grid    27
Attention      "Select 'Disagree' for this line" failed          19
Open ends      gibberish or copy-paste ("dfgdfg", "good good")   12
Duplicates     same panel ID or same answers twice                3
Removed (one or more flags; some respondents have several)       84
Kept                                                          1,040
Rule: flags agreed with the panel before fieldwork; replacements
completed to keep the quotas full
example.note: 84 interviews removed out of 1,124: reported in the method slide, and replaced so the quotas stay full.

lessons.title: Analysis: frequencies, cross-tabs, weighting and indices
text: The first output of a survey is the frequency table (in French, tri à plat): for each question, the number and the percentage of respondents who gave each answer, always with the base (who was asked). The base changes with filters: “45 % of buyers” and “45 % of all respondents” are not the same figure. Check the frequencies first: they reveal errors in filters, codes and cleaning before anyone reads a conclusion.

Cross-tabs (tri croisé) break a question down by another one, usually by target groups in columns: age, region, buyers and non-buyers. Read column percentages (“55 % of 18-34 year-olds would buy”) to compare groups. Institutes deliver “tables” with all questions crossed by the main groups, the bases and significance letters: a letter next to a figure means it is significantly higher than the column with that letter. Scales are often summarised as top 2 box (the two best answers) and bottom 2 box.

Weighting (redressement) corrects the sample’s structure so that it matches the population: if 18-34 year-olds are 30 % of the target but 40 % of the sample, each of them gets a weight below 1 and older respondents a weight above 1. Weights are computed from the population figures on the quota variables. Heavy weights (some respondents counting for three or four people) reduce the effective sample size and make results unstable; when you need them, the sample design was the real problem.

Is a difference between two groups real or noise? Test the difference between two proportions rather than comparing margins of error by eye; the statistics course explains the test. Worked example: 45 % of 400 women vs 38 % of 400 men would buy. The difference of 7 points gives z ≈ 2.0, just above 1.96, so it is significant at 95 %. The same 7 points with 100 people per group would not be. With dozens of cross-tabs, some differences will look significant by chance: focus on those that are large, consistent and linked to the research questions.

Marketing studies also use indices. The Net Promoter Score asks “How likely are you to recommend…?” on 0 to 10: promoters answer 9-10, passives 7-8, detractors 0-6, and NPS = % promoters − % detractors, from −100 to +100. CSAT is the share of satisfied customers on a satisfaction scale; Customer Effort Score measures how easy it was to get something done. Track any index with the same question, scale and method over time, and always look at the reasons behind it.
points: Frequencies (tri à plat) first, always with the base.
Cross-tabs: read column percentages; letters show significant differences.
Weighting (redressement) matches the sample to the population; heavy weights cost precision.
Test the difference between two proportions; the statistics course covers the test.
NPS = % promoters (9-10) − % detractors (0-6).

example.code:
Q12 Would you buy this dessert?    Total   18-34   35-49   50-65
                                            (A)     (B)     (C)
Base: all respondents (unweighted)  1,000   300     350     350
Definitely would buy                 14 %    18 %C   14 %    10 %
Probably would buy                   32 %    37 %C   31 %    28 %
Top 2 box (would buy)                46 %    55 %BC  45 %    38 %
Letters: significantly higher than the column with that letter (95 %)
NPS = % promoters (9-10) - % detractors (0-6)
480 promoters, 320 passives, 200 detractors -> 48 % - 20 % = NPS +28
example.note: Only 55 % among 18-34 is significantly higher than both other columns. NPS is a difference of percentages, not a percentage.

lessons.title: Classic studies: U&A, concept tests, price, awareness, satisfaction
text: A usage and attitudes study (U&A) maps a market: who buys and uses the category, how often, where, which brands, with what motivations and barriers. It is a large study run every few years or before entering a market, and it feeds segmentation and positioning. Its output is often a set of consumer segments with their size, which later studies reuse.

Concept and product tests measure the appeal of an idea or a product before launch. A concept board (a picture, a short text, a price) is shown and rated on purchase intent (typically a 5-point scale from “Definitely would buy” to “Definitely would not buy”), uniqueness, credibility and liking, with open questions on what people like and dislike. In a monadic test each respondent sees one concept only, which avoids comparisons that do not happen in real life; in a sequential monadic test each sees several, in rotated order, which needs fewer respondents. Declared purchase intent overstates real purchases, so compare it with benchmarks of past tests rather than reading it at face value.

Price sensitivity can be explored with the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter: four questions ask at what price the product would be too cheap to trust its quality, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive. The cumulative curves of answers cross at points that give a range of acceptable prices. It is simple and useful early on, but respondents do not compare with competitors’ prices; conjoint analysis and price tests in market give a more realistic view when the stakes are high.

Brand awareness has levels, always asked in this order. Spontaneous (unaided) awareness: “Which brands of … do you know, even if only by name?”; the first brand named is top of mind. Aided (prompted) awareness: the respondent sees a list and says which ones they know. Then come consideration, purchase and preference: the brand funnel. Asking aided awareness first would make spontaneous awareness meaningless.

Satisfaction and NPS barometers follow customers over time, often after a purchase or a contact with customer service (transactional) or once or twice a year (relational). The key is stable methodology, enough responses per period and per team, and a loop that brings verbatims and alerts to the teams who can act. A barometer that nobody uses to change anything becomes a reporting ritual.
points: U&A maps a market: users, habits, brands, motivations and barriers.
Concept test: purchase intent, uniqueness and liking; monadic vs sequential monadic.
Van Westendorp: four price questions give a range of acceptable prices.
Awareness: spontaneous (top of mind first) before aided.
Satisfaction barometers need a stable method and a loop to the teams who act.

example.code:
PRICE SENSITIVITY (Van Westendorp), asked for one product
At what price would you consider it ...
1. so cheap that you would doubt its quality?        (too cheap)
2. a bargain, a good buy for the money?              (cheap)
3. getting expensive, but you would still consider it? (expensive)
4. so expensive that you would not consider it?      (too expensive)
-> cumulative curves; their crossings give an acceptable price range
BRAND AWARENESS (always in this order)
Spontaneous: Which brands of plant-based desserts do you know,
             even if only by name?   first brand named = top of mind
Aided:       Here is a list of brands. Which ones do you know,
             even if only by name?
example.note: The four price questions follow one another; awareness questions come before any brand is shown.

lessons.title: The study report and working with institutes
text: A study report is not a list of charts in questionnaire order. It tells a story that answers the brief: an executive summary with the recommendation first, then the evidence organised by research question, then limits and next steps, with the method and full tables in the appendix. Each slide has an action title, a full sentence that states what the reader should remember (“Concepts B and D lead among under-35s”), not a topic (“Purchase intent”).

Choose charts that make the comparison easy: horizontal bars sorted by value for lists of items, stacked bars for scales (with the top 2 box shown), lines for change over time. Show the base and the question under every chart, round percentages to whole numbers, mark significant differences consistently and use one colour to highlight the point of the slide. Verbatims from the qualitative phase or open questions make figures concrete.

State the limits honestly: sample type (online panel, quotas), period of fieldwork, small bases, declared behaviour versus real behaviour, and what the study cannot tell. Limits do not weaken a report; they protect the client from over-reading it and protect your credibility. Then make a recommendation that answers the decision of the brief, with the risks and the next step (a test in two retail chains, a second wave).

Presenting to the client is part of the job: start with the answer, keep the method short, invite questions on the findings, and prepare for the surprise result someone will challenge. After the presentation, send the deck, the tables and a short note of decisions taken.

Many companies buy studies from research institutes. In France the large ones include Ifop, Ipsos and Kantar, alongside many specialised and smaller agencies. On the client side you write the brief, compare proposals (method, sample, quality controls, timing, price, team), validate the questionnaire and the programmed survey, follow the fieldwork progress and quotas, check the tables and challenge the report before it goes to your stakeholders. Knowing the craft yourself is what lets you challenge an institute well.
points: Executive summary and recommendation first, evidence by research question, appendix last.
Action titles: a sentence with the message, not a topic.
Every chart shows the question and the base; significant differences are marked.
State the limits and end with a recommendation and next steps.
Client side: brief, compare proposals, validate the questionnaire, follow the fieldwork, challenge the report.

example.code:
STORYLINE - plant-based dessert study (12 slides + appendix)
1  Executive summary: launch concepts B and D, at 2.49 EUR for 4
2  Reminder: decision, method, sample (n = 1,000, quotas, dates)
3  Market: 1 in 4 dessert buyers already buys plant-based
4-5 Who they are, why they buy (cross-tabs + verbatims)
6-8 Concepts: B and D lead on top 2 box, significantly
9  Price: acceptable range 2.20-2.80 EUR
10 Risks and limits: online panel, declared intent overstates sales
11 Recommendation and next steps (test in 2 retail chains)
12 Appendix: questionnaire, full tables, bases, weighting
example.note: The first slide answers the brief; the limits slide comes before the recommendation, not hidden in the appendix.

items: Context, decision, research questions, target, method, deliverables, timing, budget
What the study must answer to support the decision
Existing data first: internal data, INSEE, past studies, competitors

Many people, structured questions: how many, how much
About 6-10 people, a moderator, about 2 hours

Recruitment questionnaire that checks the target and excludes insiders
A short quote in the participant’s own words
New interviews stop bringing new themes

Sample reproduces sex, age, PCS, region, town size (INSEE)
Registered volunteers: fast and cheap, not everyone
Answers far faster than the median time

pitfalls: Starting from a questionnaire instead of a decision and research questions.
Giving percentages from qualitative interviews or focus groups.
Leading or double-barrelled questions, and showing brands before asking spontaneous awareness.
Commenting on tiny bases, or reading a difference as real without testing it.
Calling data anonymous when only names were replaced by an ID (that is pseudonymisation).
Taking declared purchase intent as a sales forecast.
A report in questionnaire order with topic titles and no recommendation.

exercises.q: Sort these survey questions: biased or neutral?

groups.name: Biased
items: Don’t you agree that our new recipe tastes better?
Is our delivery fast and cheap?
Most of our customers love the new app. What do you think of it?
How much do you usually spend on desserts?

groups.name: Neutral
items: How would you rate the taste of the new recipe? (Very good … Very bad)
How satisfied are you with the delivery time?
How many times did you buy a dessert in the last 4 weeks?
Which of these brands do you know, even if only by name?

exercises.answer: Biased: a leading question, a double-barrelled one (fast and cheap), a social pressure introduction and a vague time frame with a memory effort. Neutral questions ask one thing, with a balanced scale or a precise period.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a market study in order.
steps: Agree the decision and research questions (the brief)
Qualitative phase to explore and find the right words
Fieldwork with quotas and data cleaning
Report with recommendation, presented to the client
exercises.answer: Brief → desk research → quali → questionnaire → fieldwork → analysis → report. Each step uses the previous one: the quali phase gives the answer options of the survey.

pairs: Who buys the category, how often, and why?
Which of our four recipe ideas appeals most, and to whom?
What range of prices do buyers find acceptable?
Do people know our brand without being shown it?
Are customers more willing to recommend us than last quarter?
exercises.answer: Each classic study answers one kind of marketing question; a brief often combines two of them in one questionnaire.

exercises.q: A brand wants to understand why young parents stopped buying its baby food. Nothing is known yet. Which first field step fits best?
options: In-depth interviews with lapsed young parents
An NPS barometer of current buyers
exercises.answer: When the reasons are unknown, a qualitative phase explores them in the parents’ own words. A survey can then measure how widespread each reason is.

exercises.q: A survey of 1,000 people gives 50 %. With the same method, about how many respondents do you need to halve the margin of error?
exercises.answer: The margin shrinks with the square root of n: halving it takes four times the sample, from ±3.1 points with 1,000 to about ±1.6 with 4,000.

exercises.q: In C2, compute the margin of error at 95 % for the share of respondents who said yes (as a proportion, e.g. 0.034).
exercises.hint: The share is B2/A2. Margin = 1.96 × √(p(1 − p)/n).
exercises.explain: p = 336 / 800 = 0.42, so the margin is 1.96 × √(0.42 × 0.58 / 800) ≈ 0.034, ±3.4 points: the true share is probably between about 38.6 % and 45.4 %.

exercises.q: In D2, compute the NPS from the counts of promoters, passives and detractors (as a score, e.g. 14).
exercises.hint: NPS = % promoters − % detractors, on the total of all respondents, × 100.
exercises.explain: (210 − 140) / 500 × 100 = 14. Passives count in the total even though they are not in the difference.

exercises.q: In E2, compute the share of 18-34 year-olds who would buy (a column percentage of the cross-tab, as a proportion).
exercises.hint: Count the 18-34 who said Yes, then divide by all 18-34 respondents. COUNTIFS takes pairs of range and condition.
exercises.explain: 4 of the 6 respondents aged 18-34 said Yes: 0.667, or 67 %. The base is the column (the 18-34), not all respondents.

exercises.q: The sample over-represents under-35s. In E2, compute the yes rate weighted by the population of each segment.
exercises.hint: Each segment counts in proportion to its population: SUMPRODUCT of population and yes rate, divided by the total population.
exercises.explain: (3,000 × 0.6 + 7,000 × 0.4) / 10,000 = 0.46. Unweighted, the sample gives (180 + 80) / 500 = 0.52: the under-35s, more positive, weighed too much.

exercises.q: A product manager asks you on Monday for “a survey of 5,000 people in 3 days” about a new product nobody has seen yet.

choices.label: Ask what decision the results will support, by when, and for which target
choices.feedback: The decision and the target decide the method and the sample. Maybe 5,000 people are not needed at all.

choices.label: Open the survey tool and start writing questions
choices.feedback: Without research questions you will write a long questionnaire that does not answer the real decision.

steps.text: The decision is to choose between two concepts for a test in stores. What sample do you propose?

choices.label: About 1,000 people from an online panel with quotas, enough base per concept and for the main sub-groups
choices.feedback: With 500 per concept in a monadic test, each result has a margin of about ±4.4 points, enough to compare the concepts and the target groups.

choices.label: 5,000 people as asked, whatever it costs
choices.feedback: Five times the cost for a margin of about ±2 points per concept that the decision does not need.

steps.text: Three days is tight. How do you protect quality?

choices.label: A short questionnaire, a pilot on the first answers, cleaning rules agreed with the panel and the limits stated in the report
choices.feedback: A soft launch catches broken filters early, and the report says the study measures declared intent.

choices.label: Skip the pilot and the cleaning to save time
choices.feedback: Speeders and broken filters then end up in the figures that decide the launch.

exercises.answer: Turn the request into a brief (decision, target, timing), size the sample on the decision and the sub-groups, and protect quality with a short questionnaire, a pilot and agreed cleaning rules.

exercises.q: Write a 10-question online questionnaire for a supermarket brand that wants to know whether its customers would buy a new range of plant-based desserts. Give the questions with their answer options and say where the filters are.
exercises.answer: Example: Q1 Sex, Q2 Age band (18-24 / 25-34 / 35-49 / 50-65) and Q3 Region, for the quotas. Q4 In the last 4 weeks, did you buy a dessert in a supermarket? (Yes / No; No = end of survey). Q5 Which brands of plant-based desserts do you know, even if only by name? (open, spontaneous awareness). Q6 Here is a list of brands: which ones do you know? (aided awareness, multiple choice, rotated). Q7 How often do you buy plant-based desserts? (Every week / Every month / Less often / Never). Q8 [Concept shown, one per respondent] How likely would you be to buy this product? (5 points, Definitely would … Definitely would not). Q9 What do you like or dislike about it? (open). Q10 How would you rate its price of 2.49 EUR for 4? (Much too expensive … Very cheap, 5 points). Each question serves the decision, the scales are balanced and labelled, spontaneous awareness comes before the list, and the questionnaire takes under 10 minutes.

interview.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative research, and when do you use each?
interview.a: Qualitative research works with a few people in depth, through interviews or focus groups, to understand motivations, perceptions and vocabulary: it answers why and how, and gives no percentages. Quantitative research uses a structured questionnaire with a sample large enough to measure how many and how much. I often combine them: qualitative first to explore and find the right answer options, then a survey to size what we found, or qualitative after a survey to understand a surprising number.

interview.q: A marketing manager asks you for a survey. How do you start?
interview.a: I ask what decision the results will support and by when, then write the research questions with them, check what desk research and past studies already tell us, and only then choose the method, target and sample. I write it down as a brief so that we agree on deliverables, timing and budget before any question is written.

interview.q: How do you write questions without bias?
interview.a: One idea per question, neutral wording with no hint of the expected answer, balanced and labelled scales, precise time frames such as the last 4 weeks, exhaustive answer lists that do not overlap, and “Don’t know” when relevant. I also watch the order: spontaneous awareness before aided, general before detailed, rotation of lists. And I always pilot the questionnaire on a few people before launch.

interview.q: What is the quota method, and what is its limit?
interview.a: The sample is built to reproduce the structure of the target population on a few variables known from INSEE data, usually sex, age, occupation (PCS), region and size of town. It is the standard method for consumer surveys in France because it is fast and affordable. Its limit is that selection is not random within each cell, so the margin of error is only an approximation, and people who agree to answer, often panel volunteers, may differ from the others on things the quotas do not control.

interview.q: Explain a margin of error to a non-specialist.
interview.a: If 50 % of 1,000 people answer yes, the true figure in the population is very probably between about 47 % and 53 %: that ±3 points is the margin of error at 95 %, from 1.96 × √(p(1 − p)/n). It shrinks slowly, as the square root of the sample: four times the sample halves it. It covers only random error, not a biased sample or a badly written question.

interview.q: How do you check the quality of survey data?
interview.a: During fieldwork I follow quotas and completion times; after it I flag speeders, straight-liners, failed attention checks, nonsense open answers and duplicates with rules agreed in advance. Then I check the frequencies, the filters (only buyers rated the product) and the bases before any analysis, and I report how many interviews were removed and replaced.

interview.q: A result in your cross-tabs looks surprising. What do you do before presenting it?
interview.a: I check the base size, the filter and the wording of the question, whether the difference is significant, and whether it is consistent with other questions and with past studies or internal data. If it holds, I present it with its limits and, if possible, verbatims that explain it; if it does not, I say it is a fragile signal rather than a finding.

interview.q: How do you work with a research institute?
interview.a: I write a clear brief, compare proposals on method, sample, quality controls, team, timing and price, then validate the questionnaire and the programmed survey myself by testing it. During fieldwork I follow quotas and incidence, I check the tables when they arrive, and I challenge the report so that it answers our decision with action titles and honest limits before it reaches our stakeholders.
